title: CardVault by Tom Brady adds investors including Aaron Judge, Jay-Z, Connor McDavid
content:
Sports card retail chain CardVault by Tom Brady announced its first strategic investor group Thursday, with key players from across tech and entertainment as well as professional sports leagues including the NBA, NFL, NHL, MLB and UFC. Notable investors include New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge, Edmonton Oilers captain Connor McDavid, musician and entrepreneur Jay-Z, Fenway Sports Group owner John Henry, The Kraft Group, Boston Celtics CEO Wyc Grousbeck and UFC president and CEO Dana White. Financial details of the investment round weren’t disclosed.

Company co-founder and managing partner Chris Costa told The Athletic the investment will help the card shop chain expand with new stores, hire more employees and strengthen technology and operating infrastructure. He added that it was important for the company to find investors who have participated in the trading card industry.

“These are folks that are in tune with this space and have been active in this space, either quietly or publicly,” Costa said. “There are some real collectors on this list, which is one of the most exciting parts for me. … This industry has been driven by passion, and it is an industry that has kind of taken itself to a next generation.

“But passion for collecting and passion for fans is at the core of our business and our industry, so making sure that is true across our investor base is incredibly important.”

Founded in 2020, CardVault has 17 locations across the United States, 14 of which have opened since the seven-time Super Bowl winner acquired a 50 percent ownership stake in the retailer in February 2025. The company plans to eventually reach 100-plus stores nationwide, with 24 locations expected by the end of the year and 40 by the end of 2027.

Where those new locations land will be a major component of the company’s expansion. So far, CardVault has put a priority on attaching itself to professional sports venues, including locations inside Boston’s TD Garden, outside Chicago’s Wrigley Field and by Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass. The company’s 17th location opens Saturday in Palo Alto, Calif., near Stanford University and Brady’s home town of San Mateo.

“Major ballparks, arenas and stadiums are a priority for us,” Costa said. “It’s always going to be a priority for us getting the fans to see cards when they’re coming to or leaving a ballpark, arena or stadium. I think it’s kind of a tier-one opportunity for our hobby to grow.”

This approach has also helped CardVault locations become a hangout spot for the growing number of athletes who have become card collectors as they travel the country. After facing each other in a day game last month, members of the Yankees and Chicago Cubs went directly to the CardVault shop across the street from Wrigley Field for a private rip session.

“We’ve also got some really exciting non-venue locations coming up to close out the year,” Costa added. “I think if you fast-forward to 50 stores, or if you want to go all the way up to 100, you’ll see a really nice balance of ballparks or stadiums, but (CardVault) has also landed in some premier high foot-traffic shopping destinations or tourist destinations.”

In addition to increasing the company’s footprint nationwide, the latest financial investment will play a major role in creating a similar experience at each of the chain’s stores, which Costa believes is critical for new hobbyists.

Costa says CardVault has a “needle to thread” while pairing the experience of a local card shop with a larger retail chain. Just as hundreds of new hobby shops have popped up nationwide in recent years, big box stores including Target, Dick’s Sporting Goods and Walmart have made significant investments to attract trading card collectors to those locations. CardVault aims to fall in the middle.

“Our industry has made humongous leaps and bounds over the last five, 10 years,” Costa said. “Well, the retail experience really hasn’t. Not a lot has changed. (CardVault) saw that as an opportunity to take what was the more educational, accessible, hobby-focused experience and do that at scale.”

Costa is also adamant that the ideal hobby experience is achieved through brick-and-mortar locations. He understands some may balk at that strategy in an increasingly digital landscape, but the hobby is largely physical, and he believes the demand has validated CardVault’s model.

“I think for us, brick-and-mortar will always remain the backbone of our space,” Costa said. “For (CardVault) to grow the space, the backbone experience has to improve and has to continue to grow and scale. So we’re taking it upon ourselves.”
